topic: Core commands: ls, cd, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, find
title: Find your way around the shell
instructions:
## Your first shell session

You are **ama**, a new technician at the polytechnic. Your home directory is a mess: files from a previous project are scattered about.

## Do this

1. Look around with `pwd`, `ls` and `ls -la`. Read `man ls` if you are unsure what the columns mean.
2. Create the directory `projects/thesis` (one command can make both levels).
3. Move the three `.md` files from your home into `projects/thesis`.
4. Copy `/etc/hostname` to `notes/hostname.txt`.
5. Delete the `old` directory and everything inside it.
6. Use `find /var/log -name "*.log"` to see the log files, then press **Check my work**.

Every command has a manual page: `man cp`, `man mv`, `man find`.

files./home/ama/proposal.md:
# Thesis proposal

A virtual lab for computer science.

hints: mkdir -p projects/thesis creates both directories in one go.
mv *.md projects/thesis moves every file ending in .md; the shell expands the star.
rm -r old removes a directory and its contents. There is no undo, so look first with ls -R old.

checks.message: proposal.md is still in your home directory. Move it (mv), do not copy it.

checks.message: The old directory is still there. rm needs -r to remove a directory.

checks.message: todo.txt should still be in your home with its contents.

checks.message: Run find /var/log -name "*.log" to list the log files.

realityNote: These commands behave the same on every Linux and on macOS. The one habit to build now: run ls before rm, and never type rm -rf / or rm -rf * without looking at where you are.
